articles.title: Pezeshkian calls environmental destruction caused by regional wars 'ecocide'
articles.summary:
Pezeshkian calls environmental destruction caused by regional wars 'ecocide'

Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian has called the destruction of ecosystems caused by the "wars of aggression" an act of "ecocide", urging the international community to establish effective and enforceable mechanisms to protect biodiversity during armed conflicts.

Addressing the Leaders’ Summit of the 17th Conference of the Parties to the Convention on Biological Diversity, held in Armenia’s Yerevan on Friday, Pezeshkian said the US-Israeli war has damaged industrial and energy facilities, caused fires and released pollutants, contaminating soil and water and threatening natural ecosystems, according to Iran's Tasnim News Agency.

Pezeshkian described the environmental devastation caused by the wars in the region, including in Gaza, as “ecocide” that must be condemned, adding that pollution and ecological damage transcend national borders, Tasnim reported.

"War not only kills people and destroys economic infrastructure but also burns forests, damages wetlands, contaminates soil, threatens water resources and destroys wildlife habitats. 

"He warned that such damage can persist for years or even generations after hostilities end," he said.

articles.title: UKMTO says most vessels don't report Hormuz attacks
articles.summary:
UKMTO says most vessels don't report Hormuz attacks

The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) has said it was struggling to establish the true number of attacks in the Strait of Hormuz because most vessels attacked were refusing to report incidents to the agency.

In its 'Voluntary Reporting Area Weekly Overview', the maritime security watchdog said that reports received through other sources could not always be verified. It also said that US-reported facilitated transit figures could not be independently verified.

Combined inbound and outbound transits through the Strait of Hormuz remained about 70 percent below pre-war levels, it said.

The UKMTO added that of the 12 vessels struck during its latest weekly reporting period--10 in Hormuz and one each in the Gulf and the Gulf of Oman--six continued their journeys or reached port, one was lost, and two were disabled or not under command.

Damage or outcomes remained unconfirmed in three cases, according to the report.

articles.title: Spanish PM says Iran war has cost Europeans more than $112 billion
articles.summary:
Spanish PM says Iran war has cost Europeans more than $112 billion

Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez has said the war on Iran has already cost Europeans more than 100 billion euros ($112bn).

“Those of us who raised our voices against the war were right when we said NO to war,” he wrote on X.

“We knew ordinary people would end up paying the bill.”

Keeping the economic toll of the war in mind, Sanchez said "that is why we have ratified in Congress a social shield of more than 12 billion euros ($13.4bn) to protect citizens and the affected sectors".

Spain’s parliament had approved a package worth more than 12 billion euros ($13.4bn) “to protect the affected sectors and also to protect citizens who use their cars”.

"Now, it's time to put an end to this disaster," he said.

Los que alzamos la voz contra la guerra teníamos razón cuando dijimos NO a la guerra. La guerra de Irán ya nos ha costado más de 100.000 millones de euros a los europeos. Sabíamos que la factura la iba a terminar pagando la gente de a pie. Por eso, hoy hemos convalidado en el Congreso un escudo social de más de 12.000 millones para proteger a los ciudadanos y a los sectores afectados. Ahora, toca poner fin a este desastre.

— Pedro Sánchez (@sanchezcastejon) October 16, 2026

articles.title: Saudi Arabia to execute man for being at protests and funerals when he was 15
articles.summary:
Use of death penalty against people for crimes committed when they were children a ‘new low’, say rights groups

A young man faces imminent execution in Saudi Arabia for attending protests and funerals when he was aged 15 to 17, say human rights groups, in the latest example of the kingdom’s surging use of the death penalty for non-violent crimes.

Youssef al-Manasif was arrested in 2017 and accused of crimes including joining demonstrations for religious freedom by the Shia minority and attending funerals that the Saudi authorities deem to be protests. He was convicted and sentenced to death by the specialised criminal court, a secretive tribunal set up for terrorism-related cases.
